title: Om mani padme hum
hook: six syllables, spun in prayer wheels and carved into stones along mountain paths

segments.voice: Yesterday, lamrim, the staircase of the path, starting from a precious human life. Your line was precious human life. Today, a sound Tibetan Buddhists send out into the world.

A brass cylinder the size of a coffee can, set on a handle. An older woman walks around a temple, turning it with a flick of the wrist, clockwise, again and again, her lips moving. Along the path outside, flat stones are stacked into walls, each carved with the same row of letters. Up on the ridge, prayer flags carry them too. Inside the cylinder, tightly rolled, is paper printed over and over with those letters. The whole landscape seems to be saying one sentence: six syllables that Tibetan Buddhists tie to compassion.
screen: `A WHEEL TURNED CLOCKWISE.` → `STONES CARVED ALONG THE PATH.` → `ONE SENTENCE, EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Om mani padme hum is a mantra, a sacred sound to be repeated, the kind of word you met back on day one hundred two. First, whose sound it is. Tibetan Buddhists connect it with Avalokiteshvara, called Chenrezig in Tibetan, the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears the cries of the world. A Mahayana scripture, the Karandavyuha Sutra, praises it at length. To say it is to turn the mind toward that compassion. Second, the words. Mani is a jewel; padma is a lotus. So a common English rendering is your line: the jewel in the lotus. That's a start, not a settled one. Scholars argue over the grammar, and Tibetan teachers often skip the translation and explain the syllables one at a time, each linked to a quality to cultivate or a kind of suffering to be freed from. Third, the wheel and the stone. Written inside a prayer wheel, the mantra is said to be sent out with every turn. Carved on a stone, it stays there for every passerby. Printed on a flag, the wind carries it. Compassion shouldn't depend on one person remembering to say it. Fourth, the picture. The lotus grows up out of mud and opens clean, an image teachers use for a mind that stays open in a messy world. The jewel is something precious that was there all along. You don't need to settle the grammar to hold both pictures.
screen: `THE SOUND OF COMPASSION.` · `JEWEL, LOTUS, AND A GRAMMAR DEBATE.` · `SPUN, CARVED, CARRIED BY WIND.` · `A LOTUS OUT OF MUD.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say the mantra softly, om mani padme hum, at an easy, steady pace, the way it's said in Tibetan homes and temples. If saying it doesn't fit you, listen to it inwardly, or rest with the breath and the picture of a lotus opening above muddy water. There's nothing to achieve; let the sound, or the quiet, do the work.
Om mani padme hum. The mantra of compassion in Tibetan Buddhism, linked to Chenrezig, spun in wheels and carved in stone. Often rendered the jewel in the lotus. Today's word.
Your line: the jewel in the lotus. Something precious, open in the mud. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite om mani padme hum on prayer beads, turn prayer wheels that contain it, and carve or print it on stones and flags, as an expression of the compassion of Chenrezig.

chat.says: Why do Tibetan Buddhists put that mantra on wheels and stones, instead of just saying it?
options: So compassion goes out with every turn, stone and flag, not only when someone remembers.
Because only monks may say the mantra aloud, so lay people turn wheels instead.
Because the carvings mark the edges of temple land, like old boundary stones.
chat.meaning: Om mani padme hum is the mantra of compassion. Spun in wheels, carved in stone and printed on flags, it keeps going without one person remembering to say it.
